pillar_reactions.evidence: The prospect promoted the pillar himself, unprompted, to the top of his own list: 'the mobility part, as I said, I think is — I'm gonna place mobility as the number one thing right now for me because I'm really feeling it.' He then extended the rep's imbalance explanation with his own experience: 'a lot of the exercises that I was doing, where it was supposed to actually fire the glutes, it didn't. And of course your lower back takes a lot of that pressure.' Strongest pillar reaction in the batch so far.

Asked twice for mechanics — 'When you say nutrition, what do you mean? Is it like, I have a meal plan for you, or...?' — and on hearing it was guidelines rather than a weighed plan, confirmed the fit in his own terms: 'honestly, I would hate to do that. I'd like to eat within a specific guideline, but... I want to still enjoy that, basically.' The weekly cheat meal landed well: 'Go have a curry, or go get a Sunday roast.'

He had already named accountability as his single biggest need before the pillar was presented — 'if there's no one holding me accountable, I'll just do nothing' — and then interrogated the mechanism: 'A question here. What data do you look at? And how do you measure?', followed by asking whether his Garmin data could feed in. Engaged and practical rather than sold; the rep answered on app logging, weight, time and form videos.

anchors.raw: So, like I said, I got these ghetto belts, I got a 4, 8, and a 12, right?... I mean, I went to YouTube, that's where I actually got hold of what you guys are doing, and there's so many things out there
anchors.note: He already owns the equipment — 4kg, 8kg and 12kg kettlebells plus a TRX in storage — and found the company through free instructional content he was already using. Everything physical he needs is in his house, so £4,400 buys coaching and accountability only. The rep never explicitly reframed the price against that, which matters because the prospect had already identified accountability as the thing he is actually missing.

anchors.raw: I tried joining this JD gym, it just didn't work for me, and so forth, and of course I've gained 10 kilograms as a result of it
anchors.note: His most recent fitness spend was a budget UK gym chain membership, abandoned after roughly five minutes of stepping left him 'half dead'. That is the reference point for what he has historically been willing to pay for fitness, and it is two orders of magnitude below the offer.

anchors.raw: And there's the other thing. If you, if you don't have skin in the game, suddenly the commitment level isn't the, you know what I'm saying?
anchors.note: Volunteered by the prospect immediately after hearing the payment structure. He believes paying meaningfully is what will make him do the work, which is the single strongest price-supporting signal in the batch and directly answers his own stated accountability gap. The rep did not build on it.

unmet_demand.want: Preparation specifically for returning to cycling, his primary sport for thirty years, with the possibility of racing — 'I'm basically preparing myself for when the bikes come out' and 'possibly even do a race here or two'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The offer is kettlebells, mobility and nutrition. Nothing was said about how the programme integrates with, or programmes around, ten-plus hours a week of riding once the bikes come out of storage, which is expected within a month. The rep positioned kettlebell conditioning as 'more so like sprinting cardio than it is running or cycling' without connecting it to the prospect's actual sport, and his existing 50km a month of walking was never incorporated either.

unmet_demand.want: Short, frequent sessions — 'some form of like 10 to maybe 15 minutes of exercise' every second day
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The prescribed dose is four sessions a week at 20 to 45 minutes, roughly double what he asked for in both length and weekly volume. The rep stated the real numbers plainly and the prospect accepted without pushback, but the request itself was never revisited or reconciled with his eight-to-nine-hour working day.
